title: My SCUDEM Project: Modeling the AI Ouroboros Problem
text:
SCUDEM stands for SIMIODE Challenge Using Differential Equations Modeling.
It is an international student competition where small teams choose a real-world problem and build a differential equations model to describe, predict, or analyze the behavior of the system.
Teams spend several days:

reading and interpreting a modeling prompt

identifying important variables

writing differential equations

analyzing the behavior of the system

and creating a short presentation explaining their model

The challenge focuses more on creative thinking, communication, and modeling logic than on solving advanced equations. It’s a great introduction to applied mathematics.

title: My SCUDEM Project: Modeling the AI Ouroboros Problem
section: 2. The Modeling Prompt We Chose: “The AI Ouroboros”
text:
2. The Modeling Prompt We Chose: “The AI Ouroboros”
Our SCUDEM team chose a problem often called the “AI Ouroboros”, named after the mythological snake that eats its own tail.
The idea is this:

AI models (like large language models) are trained on huge datasets of human-written text.
As more content online becomes AI-generated, future AI models may accidentally train on AI-written text instead of human-written text.
Over time, this can create a feedback loop where AI is “training on itself,” potentially leading to:

less diversity in language

amplified errors

drifting quality

collapsed or unstable model behavior


This is a real concern in the AI and data science communities.
Our goal was to use differential equations to model how the proportion of AI-generated content might grow over time and how that affects long-term model quality.

title: My SCUDEM Project: Modeling the AI Ouroboros Problem
text:
3. Variables and Basic Assumptions
To simplify the problem for SCUDEM, our model focused on two main quantities:

O(t) = amount of human-generated text available at time t

n(t) = amount of AI-generated error at time t

We assumed:

People are still producing human-written text at a steady rate.

AI systems produce error occasionally, and this can be used to learn from.
There needs to be a rate of media decay.

title: My SCUDEM Project: Modeling the AI Ouroboros Problem
text:
4. The Differential Equations Modeling Process
We initially came up with equations like this:
[ (t) = SaU - Sm ]
[ (AI) = I(Human) + I(Prompt) + I(New) ]
Here, we tried to come up with equations by ourselves and reason through it along, but it did not work. We had to work together, plan steps and phases of the project, build a roadmap and and eventually, an equation. That euqation we came up with (after many cups of coffee):
[ O’(t) = kO(t) + bn’(t) ]

O’(t) = Total AI output rate.
O(t) = Pool of human produced content.
k = Some constant to effect the growth of the total pool.

n’(t) = AI entropy, or error.
b = rate at which we learn and create new content from AI error.

title: My SCUDEM Project: Modeling the AI Ouroboros Problem
section: 5. Analysis and Behavior of the System
text:
5. Analysis and Behavior of the System
Observations:
Our model suggests that if k remains high and b remains positive, O(t) will continue to grow, representing rapid cultural and informational expansion. However, if AI feedback dominates without human correction (negative b), the model can predict stagnation, where originality it decreased over time.

title: My SCUDEM Project: Modeling the AI Ouroboros Problem
text:
6. What Our Team Learned
Working on this problem helped our team learn:

how to build simple differential equations from a real-world situation

how feedback loops can cause systems to collapse or reach equilibrium

how exponential vs linear growth affects long-term model behavior

how even small parameter changes can drastically change outcomes

how to present mathematical ideas clearly with graphs and explanations

It also introduced us to an important topic in AI ethics and safety:
the importance of preserving human-written data and monitoring model training sources.

title: My SCUDEM Project: Modeling the AI Ouroboros Problem
text:
7. Conclusion
Our SCUDEM project on the AI Ouroboros helped us understand how differential equations can model real-world problems—even modern ones involving artificial intelligence. Completing SCUDEM helped me understand how mathematical modeling connects abstract systems to real human questions and how differential equations can describe not only motion or decay, but also the dynamics of knowledge itself.

title: What Is OpenCV? A Simple Overview for Beginners
text:
OpenCV stands for Open Source Computer Vision Library.
It is one of the most widely used tools for working with images and video using code.
Computer vision is a field of computer science that focuses on helping computers see and understand the world through cameras, just like humans do with their eyes. OpenCV gives programmers hundreds of tools to:

load images

detect shapes

recognize faces

track moving objects

filter/blur images

understand edges and lines

work with cameras in real time

OpenCV works in languages like Python, C++, and Java, but Python is the easiest way to start.

title: What Is OpenCV? A Simple Overview for Beginners
text:
2. What Can OpenCV Do?
OpenCV contains thousands of functions, but here are some of the most common things beginners use it for.

1. Reading and writing images
OpenCV can open a photo from your computer, process it, then save the result.


2. Drawing and editing
You can add text, shapes, or colors to images through programming.


3. Filtering (blurring, sharpening, smoothing)
Want to blur a background like portrait mode?
OpenCV can do that with a single function call.


4. Edge detection
OpenCV can find edges, lines, and corners. This is extremely useful for robotics and self-driving cars.


5. Working with webcams
OpenCV can capture live video from your computer’s camera and analyze each frame as it comes in.


6. Detecting faces, eyes, hands, or objects
Although OpenCV is not a “deep learning” library itself, it integrates with AI models and includes prebuilt detectors for common objects.


7. Object tracking
You can track a moving ball, a person walking through a room, or a car driving across a video frame.
Even though most high-end vision tasks now use deep learning (like TensorFlow or PyTorch), OpenCV is still the backbone for basic image handling and processing.

title: What Is OpenCV? A Simple Overview for Beginners
text:
3. Installing OpenCV in Python
If you ever want to try OpenCV in Python, installation is simple:
```bash pip install opencv-python

title: What Is OpenCV? A Simple Overview for Beginners
section: 4. A Tiny Example: Reading and Showing an image
text:
4. A Tiny Example: Reading and Showing an image
Here is a simple code example to demonstrate how OpenCV works. It loads an image (called my_image.jpg for this example) and displays it in a window.
import cv2
img = cv2.imread(“my_image.jpg”)
cv2.imshow(“My Image”, img)
cv2.waitKey(0)
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

title: What Is OpenCV? A Simple Overview for Beginners
section: 4. Another Example: Converting an Image to Grayscale
text:
4. Another Example: Converting an Image to Grayscale
A common beginner operation is turning a color image into grayscale:
import cv2
img = cv2.imread(“my_image.jpg”) gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
cv2.imshow(“Grayscale”, gray) cv2.waitKey(0) cv2.destroyAllWindows()
This is helpful for things like edge detection, shape recognition, and preprocessing before applying machine learning.

title: What Is OpenCV? A Simple Overview for Beginners
text:
6. Why Is OpenCV Important?
OpenCV is important because it acts as the foundation of countless vision projects. Even if you later use advanced AI models, you will almost always use OpenCV for: - Loading and resizing images - Converting colors - Cropping and Drawing - Preparing input for deep learning models - Capturing frames from webcam streams
Companies like Tesla, Meta, Google, Adobe, and robotics teams everywhere use OpenCV for various tasks.

title: Using Google Gemini from Python
text:
Google Gemini is an AI assistant created by Google. It can help with writing, explaining topics, summarizing articles, planning assignments, and even helping you understand Python code.
You can talk to Gemini through a website, a mobile app, or through Python code using an API (Application Programming Interface). An API lets your program “talk” to Gemini and receive answers.
In this guide, we’ll walk through how a high school student with basic Python experience can:

Set up or sign into a Google account

Get a Gemini API key from Google AI Studio

Install the required Python package

Write a very small Python script that sends a question to Gemini

Print Gemini’s response in the terminal

title: Using Google Gemini from Python
section: 2. Creating or Signing Into a Google Account
text:
2. Creating or Signing Into a Google Account
If you already have Gmail, YouTube, or Google Docs, you already have a Google account.
If not, follow these steps:

Go to https://accounts.google.com

Click Create account

Choose For my personal use

Fill out the basic information (name, birthday, etc.)

You’ll receive a Google email address like yourname@gmail.com

You will use this account to sign into Google AI Studio, where the Gemini API is managed.

title: Using Google Gemini from Python
text:
3. Getting Your Gemini API Key
A Gemini API key is like a “password” that your Python code uses to access Gemini.
Never post it publicly.

Steps to get your key:

Go to Google AI Studio: https://aistudio.google.com

Sign in with your Google account

Accept any terms or permissions if prompted

In the left sidebar, find API Keys

Click Create API key

Copy the key somewhere safe

Your key will look something like: AlzaSyA3e for example
We will NOT paste the real key into our Python code, but we will show where it goes.

title: Using Google Gemini from Python
text:
4. Installing the Python Package (google-genai)
To talk to Gemini from Python, Google provides the official google-genai package.
Open your terminal and run:
```bash pip install google-genai
Or if that doesn’t work, (as in more that one copy of python installed)
```bash python -m pip install google-genai

title: Using Google Gemini from Python
section: 5. Setting Up Your API KEy in Your terminal
text:
5. Setting Up Your API KEy in Your terminal
We need to give your Python script access to the API key. The safest way is to store it in an environment variable.
In your terminal, type:
export GEMINI_API_KEY = “your API key here”
This only lasts while the terminal is open. If you close the windown, you’ll need to run it again later.

title: Using Google Gemini from Python
section: 6. A Python Script tpo Query Gemini
text:
6. A Python Script tpo Query Gemini
This code will load your API key, create a Gimini client, send a simple question, and then print Gemini’s answer.
Save this as gemini_demy.py:
from google import genai import os
def main(): # Load the API key from the environment api_key = os.environ.get(“GEMINI_API_KEY”) if not api_key: raise RuntimeError(“GEMINI_API_KEY environment variable is not set.”)
# Create a Gemini client
client = genai.Client(api_key=api_key)

# Ask Gemini a simple question
response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    contents="Explain what an API is to a high school student."
)

# Print the response
print("Gemini says:\n")
print(response.text)
if name == “main”: main()
You can run this code with:
```bash python gemini_demo.py
If everything is set up correctly, Gemini will print a helpful explanation.

title: Using Google Gemini from Python
text:
7. More Example Queries
Once the basic script works, you can try different questions.
Here is code that ask Gemini to explain Python lists:
response = client.models.generate_content( model=“gemini-2.5-flash”, contents=“Explain Python lists with a simple example.” ) print(response.text)
And here is code that asks Gemini for homework/study help:
response = client.models.generate_content( model=“gemini-2.5-flash”, contents=“Give me three study tips for learning Python.” ) print(response.text)

title: Using Google Gemini from Python
text:
8. Summary
In this tutorial, we created or signed into a Google account, retrieved a GeminiAPI key from Google AI Studio, Installed the gogle-ganai package, set up your AIP key in the terminal, wrote some small python programs to query Gemini, and printed the AI’s response.
